---
title: "From probabilities to log odds"
---

The [link-function page](link-functions.qmd) used the logit to connect a Bernoulli probability to a real-valued linear predictor. This page develops the odds and log-odds quantities inside that transformation.

Let $\pi$ be the probability of an *in* completion. The probability of the alternative *for* completion is $1-\pi$.

The [**odds**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) compare these two probabilities:

$$
\operatorname{odds}(\pi)
=\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}.
$$

The numerator corresponds to the modeled event. The denominator corresponds to its complement.
If the event coding is reversed, the odds become their reciprocal. The direction of an odds comparison thus depends on which event appears in the numerator.

## Converting several probabilities

| probability $\pi$ | complement $1-\pi$ | odds $\pi/(1-\pi)$ |
|---:|---:|---:|
| $.20$ | $.80$ | $.25$ |
| $.50$ | $.50$ | $1$ |
| $.80$ | $.20$ | $4$ |

Odds of $.25$ mean one expected event for every four expected nonevents. Odds of 4 mean four expected events for every one expected nonevent.

Probabilities range from 0 to 1. Odds range from 0 to infinity.

Odds are not probabilities. Odds 4 correspond to probability $.8$, not to a
probability of 4. To convert odds $o$ back to probability, solve

$$
o=\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}
$$

for $\pi$:

$$
\pi=\frac{o}{1+o}.
$$

Thus odds $.25$ give probability $.25/1.25=.20$, and odds 4 give probability
$4/5=.80$.

## Taking the logarithm

The [**log odds**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214), or [**logit**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214), are

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi)
=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}.
$$

For the three probabilities:

| $\pi$ | odds | log odds |
|---:|---:|---:|
| $.20$ | $.25$ | $-1.386$ |
| $.50$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $.80$ | $4$ | $1.386$ |

Log odds span the real line. Probabilities below $.50$ produce negative log odds, $.50$ produces zero, and probabilities above $.50$ produce positive log odds.

This range makes log odds suitable for a linear predictor.

Taking the logarithm also turns reciprocal odds into sign reversals. If the odds
of *in* are 4, the odds of *for* are $1/4$. Their log odds are $1.386$ and
$-1.386$. Reversing the modeled event is thus visible as a coefficient-sign reversal on the logit scale.

## Transforming back to probability

Solve

$$
\eta=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}
$$

for $\pi$. The inverse logit is

$$
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta)
=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}.
$$

It maps every real $\eta$ into a probability between zero and one.

We can verify the round trip:

```{r}
#| label: verify-odds-logit-round-trip
#| echo: true
probability <- c(.20, .50, .80)
odds <- probability / (1 - probability)
log_odds <- log(odds)
recovered_probability <- plogis(log_odds)

data.frame(
  probability = probability,
  odds = odds,
  log_odds = log_odds,
  recovered_probability = recovered_probability
)
```

`plogis()` is R's inverse-logit function. The recovered probabilities equal the
original values up to numerical precision.

## Interpreting an additive change

Suppose log odds increase by $\beta$:

$$
\log\operatorname{odds}_2
=\log\operatorname{odds}_1+\beta.
$$

Exponentiating gives

$$
\operatorname{odds}_2
=e^\beta\operatorname{odds}_1.
$$

Thus adding $\beta$ to log odds multiplies odds by $e^\beta$.

Suppose $\beta=\log2\approx.693$. Then a one-unit predictor increase doubles the
odds. If the starting probability is $.20$, the starting odds are $.25$.
Doubling gives odds $.50$, which correspond to probability

$$
\frac{.50}{1+.50}=.333.
$$

The probability change is about $.133$.

If the starting probability is $.70$, the starting odds are

$$
\frac{.70}{.30}\approx2.333.
$$

Doubling gives odds about 4.667 and probability

$$
\frac{4.667}{1+4.667}\approx.824.
$$

The probability change is about $.124$. The odds multiplier is 2 in both cases,
but the probability difference depends on the starting point.

## Distinguishing an odds ratio from a probability ratio

For the first comparison, the probability ratio is

$$
.333/.20\approx1.665,
$$

while the odds ratio is 2. These are different summaries and should not be
conflated.

An odds ratio can be constant across predictor values under logistic regression
while probability ratios and probability differences vary. A report should state
which summary it uses and provide response-scale probabilities for the
linguistic profiles of interest.

The task is included because several theoretically meaningful coefficients combine on the log odds scale, while the linguistic comparison is easier to understand on the probability scale.
:::

Odds compare an event with its complement, while log odds place that comparison on the real line. A fixed additive change in log odds is a fixed odds multiplier, not a fixed probability change.
